key: When we can lay hold of the Tao of old to direct the things of the present day, and are able to know it as it was of old in the beginning, this is called (unwinding) the clue of Tao.
s: Closing a chapter on the invisible, the verse joins past and present; Wang Bi, on chapter 14, takes that Tao as the formless, nameless ancestor of all things, through which every age achieves order however customs change, so the ancient beginning is knowable now.
src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 14, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

evidence.words: 無形無名者，萬物之宗也。雖今古不同，時移俗易，故莫不由乎此以成其治者也。…上古雖遠，其道存焉，故雖在今，可以知古始也。
evidence.gloss: What is without form and without name is the ancestor of all things. Though present and past differ, and times shift and customs change, none fails to follow it in achieving its order. … Though high antiquity is remote, its Tao remains; so even now one can know the ancient beginning.
